claims.text: Mössbauer spectroscopy can detect the presence of ferromagnetic ground states in materials.
The material being measured is initially ferromagnetic.
The proposed intervention is a Mössbauer spectroscopy measurement.
The measurement should be performed at low temperature.
An applied magnetic field is a condition of the measurement.
Magnetic moment is the structural mediator linking the measurement to identification of ferromagnetism.
The operative mechanism is nuclear gamma resonance absorption.
Mössbauer spectroscopy is predicted to detect a ferromagnetic ground state.
A non-ferromagnetic material serves as the baseline.
Temperature above the Curie point is a boundary condition for the proposed detection.
The method is limited to materials containing Mössbauer-active nuclei.
Iron is an example of an element with Mössbauer-active nuclei.
Failure to observe signs of a ferromagnetic ground state in a known non-ferromagnetic material would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The absence of a ferromagnetic signature in a known non-ferromagnetic control is consistent with the hypothesis rather than a falsification of it.

Using an applied magnetic field may induce or align magnetization, while the stated outcome is detection of an intrinsic ferromagnetic ground state; the hypothesis does not explain how these effects would be distinguished.
